speaker: youngPlato
text: Shh, I'm writing. Socrates never writes anything down. He says writing makes memory lazy!

speaker: youngPlato
text: So I'll write *dialogues*: little plays starring him. Ironically, the only reason anyone will remember him is my books.

speaker: youngPlato
text: One day I'll found a school called the *Academy*. Our word "academic" will come from it. It'll run for about 300 years.

speaker: sophist
text: Psst! I'm *Gorgias*, a Sophist. For a fee I'll teach you to win *any* argument, whether you're right or not!

speaker: sophist
text: Special price: two obols. What do you say?

speaker: sophist
text: Lesson one: never admit you're wrong. Lesson two: if you're losing, *talk faster*. Lesson three: see lesson one.

speaker: socrates
text: (from across the square) And what if the other person is *right*, Gorgias? Then you've "won" and stayed foolish!

speaker: sophist
text: Bah! You sound just like Socrates. He never charges a single coin. Terrible business model.

speaker: owl
text: The Sophists taught *rhetoric*, the art of persuasion. Socrates cared about *truth* instead. That's why "sophistry" now means clever-sounding but misleading arguments.

speaker: narrator
text: Citizens gather here to argue about politics, trade gossip and buy olives.

speaker: owl
text: Athens invented *democracy*: "rule by the people." Citizens voted directly on laws. But only free adult men counted. Women, slaves and foreigners had no vote. A good question for Socrates: *was that just?*

speaker: socrates
text: Still here? Good. Keep asking questions. When someone says "everyone knows that…", that's exactly where to dig.

speaker: socrates
text: Ah, a new face! I'm Socrates. I don't teach anything. I just ask questions. Will you help me with one?

speaker: socrates
text: Here it is: *What is justice?*

speaker: socrates
text: What is justice? Give me your best answer.

speaker: socrates
text: Hmm. Then try again: *what is justice?*

speaker: you
text: Hmm… okay, maybe not quite.

speaker: you
text: Ugh. You're good at this.

speaker: you
text: Hmm…

speaker: you
text: Wait… then I don't know what justice is at all!

speaker: socrates
text: Wonderful! Don't look so sad. You've lost a *false belief*. That's a gain, not a loss!

speaker: socrates
text: This is my method: ask "what is X?", then test each answer with *counterexamples*. People call it the *Socratic method*.

speaker: socrates
text: Most people are certain about big words like justice, courage and love, and they never check. Now you've checked. Now you *know that you don't know*. That's where real thinking begins.

speaker: socrates
text: Now. My student Plato, that young man writing everything down, will grow up with a bold idea:

speaker: socrates
text: that the true reality is *beyond* this world of the senses. And *his* student Aristotle will disagree: truth is right *here*, in real things.

speaker: socrates
text: Your road leads upper-left, to Plato's Cave.

speaker: socrates
text: Your road leads lower-left, to Aristotle's Lyceum.

speaker: socrates
text: So which road calls you? *Is truth beyond this world, or in it?*

speaker: socrates
text: Then go upper-left, to the Cave. Bring a sense of wonder… and maybe sunglasses.

speaker: socrates
text: Then go lower-left, to the Lyceum. Aristotle walks while he talks, so keep up!

speaker: owl
text: Don't worry: once you finish that road, the other one opens too. *Every* path can be explored.

speaker: narrator
text: A stone tablet: *"The Oracle of Delphi was asked: is anyone wiser than Socrates? The priestess answered: No one."*

speaker: name:Chaerephon
text: Socrates, my friend! I went all the way to Delphi and asked the god: is anyone wiser than you? The priestess said: *no one!*

speaker: socrates
text: Me? But I know *nothing*! There must be a mistake. I'll find someone wiser and prove the god wrong.

speaker: name:A Famous Politician
text: Justice? Simple. It's whatever wins votes. Next question.

speaker: name:A Celebrated Poet
text: My verses are inspired by the Muses! What do they *mean*? Well… I couldn't really say.

speaker: name:A Skilled Craftsman
text: I make the finest shoes in Athens! So of course I also know how the city should be run.

speaker: socrates
text: Each one *thought* he knew things he didn't. The craftsman truly knew his craft, but thought that made him wise about everything.

speaker: socrates
text: So I am wiser in just one tiny way: *I know that I don't know.* Maybe that's what the god meant.

speaker: owl
text: Asking experts hard questions in public made Socrates many enemies. Powerful people don't like looking foolish.

speaker: narrator
text: A cup of *hemlock*, a poison. Something terrible happened in this city…

speaker: name:Meletus, the accuser
text: Men of Athens! This Socrates *corrupts the youth* and does not honor the gods of the city! He must be punished!

speaker: narrator
text: Socrates speaks in his own defense. He doesn't beg or weep, as accused men usually did.

speaker: socrates
text: I am like a *gadfly* on a great, lazy horse. If you kill me, you won't easily find another to keep you awake. And I tell you: *the unexamined life is not worth living.*

speaker: narrator
text: A jury of about *500 citizens* votes, dropping pebbles into urns…

speaker: narrator
text: Guilty, by about 60 votes. The sentence: *death*.

speaker: name:Crito
text: Socrates, everything is ready. The guards are bribed. A ship is waiting. *Escape tonight!*

speaker: socrates
text: Dear Crito. Should I break the laws that raised me, just to save my own skin? Would that be *just*? No. I won't run.

speaker: narrator
text: The jailer brings the cup. The friends weep. Socrates comforts *them*.

speaker: socrates
text: Why cry? We have spent our lives practicing for this: caring for the soul more than the body. Let us go calmly.

speaker: narrator
text: He drank calmly, talking with his friends about the soul until the end.

speaker: owl
text: Plato was too ill to be there that day. He wrote the scene later, in the *Phaedo*. Socrates died for the right to keep asking questions.

speaker: socrates
text: Ha! Leave it be. I call *myself* a gadfly. Look:

speaker: narrator
text: Athens is like a big, noble horse: strong, but lazy and half asleep.

speaker: socrates
text: Sting! Now it's awake. Annoying? Yes. Useful? Also yes. A city that never gets questioned falls asleep.

speaker: narrator
text: Slowly, the lotus flowers open: pure pink petals rising from brown, muddy water.

speaker: owl
text: The lotus is a favorite Buddhist symbol. It grows *out of* the mud, yet blooms clean. Awakening doesn't happen by escaping life's mess. It grows *from* it.

speaker: narrator
text: The deer look up, hop a few steps, then go back to grazing.

speaker: owl
text: After his awakening, the Buddha gave his very first teaching in a *deer park* at Sarnath, to five former companions. It's called "Setting the Wheel of Dharma in Motion."

speaker: owl
text: Hoo… are you walking slower? And what's that buzzing?

speaker: narrator
text: Arms full. Heavy. Every step is an effort, and the buzzing in your ears won't stop. Go back to the Buddha.

speaker: buddha
text: …Welcome. Sit with me. I was born *Siddhartha Gautama*, a prince, in a palace full of every pleasure. My father wanted me never to see sorrow.

speaker: buddha
text: But one day I rode out beyond the palace walls, and I saw *four sights*.

speaker: buddha
text: Old age. Sickness. Death. They come to *everyone*, even princes. And then a monk, calm in the middle of it all. I left the palace that night to find out how.

speaker: buddha
text: For six years I tried the opposite of luxury: fasting until my ribs showed, sleeping on thorns. I nearly died. It didn't help either.

speaker: buddha
text: Then, so the story goes, I overheard a music teacher on a passing boat, instructing a student. Here. Tune this string.

speaker: buddha
text: Too loose, it won't sing. Too tight, it snaps. This is the *Middle Way*: not indulgence, not self-torture.

speaker: buddha
text: I ate a bowl of rice milk, sat beneath this very tree, and vowed not to rise until I understood. At dawn, I *awoke*. "Buddha" means "the awakened one."

speaker: buddha
text: Now, let me show you the root of suffering. Treasures are scattered around this garden. Go and *gather them all*.

speaker: buddha
text: Gather them *all*, every last one. Then come back to me.

speaker: buddha
text: You have everything. Wealth, power, pleasure, praise, a fine self-image. Tell me: how do you feel?

speaker: buddha
text: This is *tanha*: craving, clinging. We grab at things that cannot last, and then we suffer when they change or slip away.

speaker: buddha
text: Let go. Press *E* to set each one down.

speaker: narrator
text: …Silence. Then a single singing bowl, slowly fading. You feel light enough to float.

speaker: buddha
text: Hear how the bowl rings and fades? Every sound, every flower, every feeling, every life arises and passes away. This is *anicca*, impermanence.

speaker: buddha
text: Suffering doesn't come from things changing. It comes from *clinging* to them as if they wouldn't.

speaker: buddha
text: Let me put it the way a doctor would. My first teaching had *four truths*.

speaker: buddha
text: Don't believe me because I said it. *Test it*, like a goldsmith tests gold by rubbing and burning it. See for yourself.

speaker: owl
text: The path *east* is open, to Paris in the 1940s. Strange neighbors, I know! But they're also asking how to live with suffering and freedom.

speaker: buddha
text: Look for your "self." Is it your body? Your feelings? Thoughts? All are always changing. Ask *Nagasena* by the chariot. He explains it well.

speaker: buddha
text: To *see clearly*. Sit, breathe, and watch thoughts arise and pass like clouds. Slowly you stop being pushed around by every craving.

speaker: monk
text: I am making a sand mandala, as monks in Tibet do. Thousands of grains, placed one by one, for days or weeks. Will you help? Press *E* to pour each ring.

speaker: monk
text: Beautiful, isn't it? Look at it carefully…

speaker: monk
text: …and gone. We always sweep it away when it's finished, and pour the sand into a river.

speaker: monk
text: Not because it didn't matter. Because *everything* is like this. Making it beautifully *and* letting it go: that's the whole practice.

speaker: kisa
text: My name is Kisa Gotami. I want to tell you how I met the Buddha. It is a sad story, but it ends in peace.

speaker: kisa
text: My little son died. I couldn't accept it. I carried him from house to house, begging for medicine to bring him back.

speaker: kisa
text: The Buddha said: "Bring me a mustard seed, but only from a house where *no one has ever died*."

speaker: kisa
text: By nightfall I understood. I was not alone. Death touches everyone. I buried my son, and became a nun.

speaker: owl
text: The Buddha didn't argue with her grief. He let her *discover* impermanence for herself, and find that it connected her to everyone else.

speaker: nagasena
text: I am the monk Nagasena. A Greek king named *Milinda*, Menander, ruler of northwest India around 150 BCE, once asked me: "Who are you, really?"

speaker: nagasena
text: I asked him: "Your Majesty, how did you come here?" "By chariot," he said. "Then show me the chariot."

speaker: nagasena
text: Is the *wheel* the chariot? No. The *axle*? No. The *box*, the *pole*? No. Is the chariot something *apart* from all its parts? No!

speaker: nagasena
text: "Chariot" is a *name* for parts working together. Useful, but there's no extra chariot-thing hiding inside.

speaker: nagasena
text: So too with "Nagasena": body, feelings, perceptions, intentions, awareness, all flowing and changing. That's *anatta*, "not-self." No fixed, unchanging core.

speaker: owl
text: Remember the pond at the Crossroads? "Who is looking back?" This is the Buddhist answer: there's a *process*, not a thing. Freeing, once you stop clinging to it!

speaker: narrator
text: That night the prince took off his crown, left the palace, and set out to find the end of suffering.

speaker: kisa
text: I went to every house in the village. Everyone had a seed to give, but every family had lost someone: a parent, a child, a friend.

speaker: narrator
text: The figure you shaped: *{}*. Every label came from an action.

speaker: narrator
text: A blank, faceless figure. No name. No purpose. It is waiting to become *someone*.

speaker: narrator
text: A little jazz phrase rings out over the clink of cups.

speaker: owl
text: In Sartre's novel *Nausea*, the hero feels that existence is pointless and sticky, until he hears a jazz record, "Some of These Days." For a moment, the music feels *necessary*. Art as a tiny rescue.

speaker: narrator
text: A faded poster: *Søren Kierkegaard*, Copenhagen, 1840s. "Anxiety is the dizziness of freedom."

speaker: owl
text: Kierkegaard is often called the *father of existentialism*, though his answer was a passionate "leap of faith." His room isn't built yet. It's on the roadmap as a teaser!

speaker: narrator
text: Rain on the rooftops of Paris. Somewhere, a siren.

speaker: owl
text: During World War II, France was occupied by Nazi Germany (1940–44). Everyday choices became life-and-death: collaborate, resist, or look away. No wonder these thinkers obsessed over *freedom* and *responsibility*.

speaker: narrator
text: The espresso machine hisses. A sign over the bar reads *Café de Flore*.

speaker: owl
text: Sartre and Beauvoir practically lived at cafés like the Flore and Les Deux Magots. During the war, the cafés were heated and their hotel rooms weren't, so they wrote there all day.

speaker: owl
text: Hoo! Paris! Every road ends up here. Smell that coffee. Listen to that rain. These people are asking: *if nothing is given to us, not even our purpose, what do we do?*

speaker: sartre
text: Mm? *(puffs pipe)*

speaker: sartre
text: Too precise, too eager, like a machine. He's *playing at being a waiter*, as if that were all he could be.

speaker: sartre
text: *Bad faith* is lying to yourself about your freedom: "I had no choice." "That's just how I am." You always have a choice. Even not choosing is a choice.

speaker: sartre
text: That line from my play *No Exit* gets misread! I didn't mean people are awful. I meant: if we depend entirely on others' judgment to know who we are, *that* becomes a hell.

speaker: sartre
text: Ah, sit, sit. Jean-Paul Sartre. Writer, philosopher, terrible at being on time. Look at this paper knife on my table.

speaker: sartre
text: Before it was made, someone *designed* it, for cutting paper. Its purpose, its *essence*, came first. Then it existed.

speaker: sartre
text: Now: what is *your* purpose? Who designed *you*? I say: no one. You *exist first*, and then you define yourself by what you do. *Existence precedes essence.*

speaker: sartre
text: Don't believe me? Here: this blank figure. Let's see who it becomes. Choose for it.

speaker: sartre
text: Look! A moment ago this was nobody. Now it is {} and {}. Not because it was *born* that way: because of what it *did*.

speaker: sartre
text: And notice: at every step, you could have chosen *otherwise*. That's the frightening part. We are *condemned to be free*. No excuses, no human nature to blame, no rulebook from the sky.

speaker: sartre
text: Freedom means *responsibility*. And when you choose, you're showing what you think a human being *should* be. Heavy, eh? Hence the anguish. Hence the coffee.

speaker: beauvoir
text: Simone de Beauvoir. Do sit down. What would you like to discuss?

speaker: beauvoir
text: In *The Second Sex* (1949) I wrote: *"One is not born, but rather becomes, a woman."* The role is taught and imposed, not a fate. It can be refused and rewritten.

speaker: owl
text: That book helped spark the modern feminist movement. It's the existentialist idea, "existence precedes essence," turned toward how societies shape people.

speaker: beauvoir
text: No! That's the trap. My freedom only means something in a world with *other* free people. *"To will oneself free is also to will others free."*

speaker: beauvoir
text: Someone who is starving, or oppressed, can't exercise their freedom fully. So taking freedom seriously means fighting for *everyone's*. I called this the *ethics of ambiguity*.

speaker: beauvoir
text: Partners for fifty years, never married, each with our own lives. We read every word the other wrote. Sometimes I think people forget *I* was a philosopher too, not just "Sartre's companion."

speaker: waiter
text: Bonjour! I am a waiter. *(bows exactly 30 degrees)* A waiter is what I am. I could not possibly be anything else.

speaker: waiter
text: What will Monsieur or Madame have?

speaker: waiter
text: Café crème. *(pivot, step, step, pivot)* Coming. Precisely. As a waiter does.

speaker: waiter
text: …Error. I… am… a waiter. *(clicks heels nervously)* Please don't ask such questions.

speaker: sartre
text: (murmuring) See? *Bad faith*. He pretends his role is his whole being, so he doesn't have to face his freedom. Of course, he *is* free. He could quit tomorrow and sail to Brazil!

speaker: camus
text: Ah, my friend.

speaker: camus
text: Everyone says so! I always denied it. I don't think we "create" meaning out of nothing. I think we face the absurd honestly and live *anyway*. A small difference, but it mattered to me.

speaker: camus
text: Not violence. Revolt means refusing both despair *and* false comfort. Keep your eyes open, keep living fully: love, create, play football, swim in the sea. *"In the midst of winter, I found there was, within me, an invincible summer."*

speaker: camus
text: Albert Camus. I grew up poor in Algiers: sun, sea, football. I love life so much it hurts. And still I see the problem.

speaker: camus
text: We demand meaning. The universe answers with… silence. That clash, our cry and the silent world, I call *the absurd*.

speaker: camus
text: Some escape it with false hope. Some give up. I say: *revolt*. Live with the absurd, fully, with eyes open. Let me show you my favorite hero.

speaker: camus
text: Step into the painting with me…

speaker: camus
text: *"The struggle itself toward the heights is enough to fill a man's heart. One must imagine Sisyphus happy."*

speaker: camus
text: His rock is his thing. His task is his. And in the moment of walking back down the hill, he is *free*, and stronger than his fate.

speaker: camus
text: And down it rolls. The gods condemned Sisyphus to push it up, forever. Pointless. Like many jobs. Like many lives. Again!

speaker: camus
text: Listen: do you hear a rhythm in his effort? The task hasn't changed. *He* is starting to. Again!

speaker: camus
text: Look at his face as he walks back down. He knows the rock will roll again. He *knows*. And he whistles.

speaker: owl
text: Hoo… Sartre: you're free and responsible for what you become. Camus: life may have no given meaning, and you can live it fully anyway.

speaker: owl
text: Look who came, {name}! Everyone you met along the way.

speaker: owl
text: Notice something? Socrates questioning, the Stoics and the Buddha on letting go, Laozi's flowing water, Camus's rock… Different lands, different centuries, *similar questions*.

speaker: owl
text: Philosophy isn't a list of answers to memorize. It's a way of *walking*: wondering, questioning, testing, and choosing how to live.

speaker: owl
text: More rooms are being built: *Epicurus's Garden*, *Descartes's Stove Room*, *Kant's Clockwork Study*, the *Zen Garden*, *Ubuntu Village*… You'll find them as grey stars on the map.

speaker: sartre
text: During the war a student came to me with an impossible choice. Watch.

speaker: narrator
text: His brother had been killed in the war. His mother, alone and heartbroken, lived only for him.

speaker: name:His Mother
text: Stay with me, my son. You are all I have left.

speaker: name:A Resistance fighter
text: France needs you. Join us. Fight to free your country.

speaker: sartre
text: No rulebook could decide for him. Christian ethics says love your neighbor, but which one? Kant says never treat people merely as means, but he must fail someone.

speaker: sartre
text: I told him: *you are free, so choose*, that is, invent. Whatever he chose, he would be choosing what kind of person he was.

speaker: sartre
text: Watch the waiter.

speaker: waiter
text: I am a waiter! I bow at exactly the correct angle. I could not *possibly* be anything else!

speaker: narrator
text: A girl is born. Nothing about her is decided yet.

speaker: name:Society
text: Be quiet. Be pretty. Don't be too clever. Your job is to please others.

speaker: name:Society
text: Girls don't do philosophy, dear. Here is an apron.

speaker: narrator
text: But a role taught is not a fate. She picks up a book and walks her own way.

speaker: narrator
text: A person stands under the night sky and asks the biggest question of all.

speaker: you
text: WHY? Why am I here? What is it all *for*?

speaker: narrator
text: …The stars say nothing at all.

speaker: owl
text: Hoo. Today you might think of advertisers, propaganda, or a social media feed: someone else choosing the shadows you watch.

speaker: narrator
text: A pile of spare wooden cutouts: a horse, a tree, a jar, a bird. Flat. Crude. Painted on one side only.

speaker: narrator
text: These are what made your whole world on the wall. The "real" horse was a *shadow of a copy*.

speaker: narrator
text: The fire is real, or at least *more* real than the shadows. But it stings your eyes. After a lifetime in the dark, even firelight hurts.

speaker: owl
text: Plato says learning is often uncomfortable at first. The truth can feel like an attack on everything you're used to.

speaker: narrator
text: LIGHT! Everything is blinding white. You can't see a thing!

speaker: narrator
text: Slowly… colors. Shapes. Your eyes are adjusting.

speaker: plato
text: Easy, friend! Don't try to look at the Sun yet. You'd only be blinded again. Come here, talk to me.

speaker: narrator
text: Darkness. Cold stone. Chains on your wrists and ankles. You've been here your *whole life*. At least, that's how it feels.

speaker: narrator
text: All you have ever seen are shapes moving on the wall in front of you. Every sound seems to come *from* the wall: muffled, echoing.

speaker: name:Prisoner
text: Look, the *horse* again! I called it first!

speaker: name:Prisoner
text: And next comes the *bird*, then the *jar*. I'm the best at predicting. Everyone honors me for it.

speaker: name:Prisoner
text: Your turn, newcomer. What's the *realest* thing in the world?

speaker: name:Prisoner
text: Exactly! What else *could* there be?

speaker: name:Prisoner
text: Behind us?! Ha! There's nothing behind us. Don't talk nonsense.

speaker: narrator
text: But something itches at you. Why do the shapes always come from the same direction? What is *behind* you?

speaker: narrator
text: The chains snap! You stand, turn around, and…

speaker: narrator
text: A *FIRE*! It burns your eyes. Between you and the fire, people walk behind a low wall, carrying *wooden cutouts* above their heads.

speaker: narrator
text: The horse. The bird. The jar. They were never real. They were *shadows of puppets*. The sounds were just echoes.

speaker: owl
text: Hoo… Look around. Talk to the puppeteers. And notice the *tunnel* in the bottom-right corner, leading *up*.

speaker: narrator
text: Back in the dark. After the sunlight, you're nearly blind down here. You stumble over a rock.

speaker: name:Prisoner
text: Ha! Look at him. He went up there and came back with *ruined eyes*. He can't even see the shadows anymore!

speaker: you
text: Listen! The shadows aren't real. There's a whole world up there, and a Sun, and real horses…

speaker: name:Prisoner
text: Madness! Nobody else go up there! And if anyone tries to drag *us* up… we'll kill them.

speaker: owl
text: Plato wrote that line on purpose. He was thinking of his teacher *Socrates*, who was executed by Athens for trying to make people see.

speaker: owl
text: Plato said true education isn't pouring knowledge into empty heads. It's *turning the whole soul around*, from shadows toward the light. Nobody can do the climbing for you.

speaker: owl
text: A passage has opened on the *right side* of the cave, toward the Stoa. And the other road from the Agora is open now too!

speaker: narrator
text: In the still water: reflections of trees and clouds. Upside down, but in *color*, in *daylight*.

speaker: plato
text: Good. First reflections, then the things themselves. The eyes, like the mind, must be led *step by step*.

speaker: narrator
text: A *real horse*! Warm, breathing, smelling of grass. It snorts and nudges your hand.

speaker: narrator
text: The thing on the wall was a flat grey shadow… of a wooden copy… of *this*.

speaker: narrator
text: AAH! Too bright! Your eyes aren't ready. Start gently: the *reflections in the pond*, then the *real things*.

speaker: narrator
text: Slowly, you lift your eyes… to the *Sun*.

speaker: narrator
text: It lights up everything. It makes the grass grow and the seasons turn. Without it, you couldn't see *anything*, not even the shadows below.

speaker: plato
text: Yes! For me the Sun stands for the *Form of the Good*: the highest reality, the source of all truth and value. Come here. Let me explain.

speaker: plato
text: Welcome to the upper world! I'm Plato. I'm the one who imagined this cave. It's an *allegory*: a story where everything stands for something else.

speaker: plato
text: The cave is the world of our *senses*. The shadows are the opinions and appearances we accept without questioning.

speaker: plato
text: Your eyes need time. First look at *reflections* in the pond. Then the *real things*: that horse there. Only then, the *Sun* from the hilltop.

speaker: plato
text: Reflections first, then things, then the Sun. Step by step, like learning mathematics!

speaker: plato
text: Now. Look at these circles someone drew in the sand.

speaker: plato
text: Each one is a bit wobbly. Listen: each sounds slightly *off*. No circle anyone has ever drawn is perfect.

speaker: plato
text: Yet you *know* they're imperfect. Compared to *what*? You've never seen a perfect circle with your eyes.

speaker: plato
text: You compare them to *the Circle itself*, the *Form* of Circle. Perfect, eternal, unchanging. Not seen with the eyes, but grasped by the *mind*.

speaker: plato
text: It's the same with horses. Big ones, small ones, spotted ones all share one Form: *Horseness*. And with Beauty, and Justice. Socrates was searching for the *Form of Justice*!

speaker: plato
text: My student Aristotle will say I've got it backwards, that forms live *inside* real things, not in some other realm. Students! Always arguing.

speaker: plato
text: And now the hardest part. Go back *down* into the cave and tell the others what you've seen. The opening is on the left.

speaker: plato
text: Remember: what you see with your eyes changes and decays. What you grasp with reason, like the Forms and mathematics, lasts forever. Or so I believe!

speaker: narrator
text: A *bianzhong*: a set of bronze bells, each tuned to a different note. Some ancient sets had over 60 bells!

speaker: owl
text: For Confucius, music and ritual worked together: ritual gives *order*, music gives *harmony*. A good society needs both.

speaker: narrator
text: Gold characters on black lacquer: *Zhengming*, "the rectification of names."

speaker: confucius
text: A ruler must *act* like a ruler. A father must *act* like a father. If names don't match reality, words lose their meaning, and then nothing can be done right.

speaker: owl
text: Imagine calling a cruel king "the people's protector." Confucius thought fixing the gap between *words* and *deeds* was the first step to fixing a society.

speaker: narrator
text: In the bronze mirror, a boy is about to shove his friend. Then the image flips: the *friend* shoves *him*.

speaker: confucius
text: A student asked me: "Is there one word to guide your whole life?" I said: *shu*, "reciprocity." *Do not impose on others what you yourself do not want.*

speaker: owl
text: Versions of this "Golden Rule" appear in many traditions: Hillel in Judaism, Jesus in Christianity, the Mahabharata in Hinduism. Confucius said it around 500 BCE.

speaker: confucius
text: Once, standing by a river, I said: "It flows on like this, never stopping, day and night."

speaker: owl
text: People still debate what he meant. Time slipping away? Or steady, ceaseless effort, like the river? Maybe both!

speaker: name:Yan Hui, a student
text: I'm the Master's favorite student, Yan Hui. He never wrote a book. We students wrote down his sayings after he died. They're called the *Analects*.

speaker: name:Yan Hui, a student
text: The very first line: *"Is it not a joy to learn, and to practice what you have learned?"*

speaker: name:Yan Hui, a student
text: He taught anyone who came with even a small gift of dried meat, rich or poor. That was unusual in his time.

speaker: confucius
text: Welcome, traveler. I am Kong Qiu. My students call me Kongzi, "Master Kong." In the West you'll call me *Confucius*.

speaker: confucius
text: I lived in a time of chaos: warring states, greedy lords, broken families. I asked: how do people live *well together*?

speaker: confucius
text: My answer: society is like a set of bells. Each *relationship* is one bell. When each is in its proper place, the whole rings in *harmony*.

speaker: confucius
text: But look around. Five relationships have turned their backs on each other. Their bells hang silent.

speaker: confucius
text: Go to each pair and help them find the right way to treat one another. Listen: you'll *hear* when it's right.

speaker: confucius
text: Listen…

speaker: confucius
text: Harmony. Not sameness: five *different* notes, each in its place, sounding together.

speaker: confucius
text: The heart of it is *ren*: humaneness, warm-heartedness toward others. It starts at home and ripples outward to the village, the state, the world.

speaker: confucius
text: And *li*: ritual, courtesy, manners. Li is how ren becomes *visible*. A bow, a greeting, a respectful silence. Small acts that hold a society together.

speaker: confucius
text: The person who lives this way is a *junzi*, an exemplary person. Not by birth, but by *character*. Anyone can become one, through learning.

speaker: confucius
text: Let me teach you one piece of li. Press *B* to bow. Try it near people. You'll see they answer in kind.

speaker: owl
text: B to bow! Works everywhere in PhilWorld. The moon gate to the *east* is open now.

speaker: confucius
text: Yes, my friend?

speaker: confucius
text: The junzi seeks the cause in *himself*; the petty person seeks it in *others*. The junzi is calm and at ease; the petty person is always anxious.

speaker: owl
text: For over 2,000 years! Confucian classics became the basis of China's imperial exams, used to choose government officials from about 600 to 1905 CE.

speaker: owl
text: Today Confucian ideas still shape life in China, Korea, Japan, Vietnam and beyond. They're also hotly debated: some say they encourage too much obedience; others say they're about mutual care.

speaker: courtyardPeople
text: Hmph. Talk to the Master first.

speaker: courtyardPeople
text: Thank you. Everything feels lighter now.

speaker: courtyardPeople
text: Ah, much better. Can you hear our bell?

speaker: courtyardPeople
text: We bowed to each other this morning. It's amazing what that does.

speaker: owl
text: All five bells ring! Go tell *Confucius*!

speaker: narrator
text: Try again?

speaker: confucius
text: Music shapes the heart. Let me show you what happened when I heard the ancient *Shao* music.

speaker: confucius
text: I didn't notice the taste of meat for three months! I never imagined music could reach such perfection.

speaker: narrator
text:
*West*: Ancient Greece. Socrates, Plato, Aristotle, the Stoics… and onward to Nietzsche.
The West often asks: *What is real? What can I know?*

speaker: narrator
text:
*East*: China and India. Confucius, Laozi, the Buddha.
The East often asks: *How do I live in harmony, with others and with the world?*

speaker: narrator
text: *North*: the Existentialist Café, Paris. Both roads end there, in the 20th century.

speaker: owl
text: Of course, those are rough generalizations. Every tradition asks *all* the big questions. That's what makes comparing them fun!

speaker: narrator
text: Your reflection looks back at you, rippling.

speaker: narrator
text: Carved above the Temple of Apollo at Delphi were two words: *"Know thyself."*

speaker: narrator
text: So… who is the "you" looking back?

speaker: owl
text: Your body replaces most of its cells over the years. Are you a *new* you? Hoo! Hold that puzzle. The Buddha has thoughts about it, out East.

speaker: owl
text: Many agree! But memories fade and change. Hold that puzzle. The Buddha has a surprising answer, out East.

speaker: owl
text: Ha! Socrates would love you. Admitting you don't know is where philosophy starts.

speaker: narrator
text: You wake at a crossroads. The sun is setting. You don't quite remember how you got here…

speaker: owl
text: Hoo! A new traveler! Welcome, *{name}*.

speaker: owl
text: I'm *Glaux*, an owl of Athena, the Greek goddess of wisdom. Owls have been a symbol of philosophy for over 2,000 years.

speaker: owl
text: A philosopher named Hegel wrote that "the owl of Minerva spreads its wings only with the falling of dusk." Wisdom often arrives *after* the day is done, when we look back.

speaker: owl
text: Fitting, isn't it? Look at that sunset.

speaker: owl
text: Tell me: have you ever wondered *why there is something rather than nothing?*

speaker: owl
text: Then you're already a philosopher. Hoo hoo!

speaker: owl
text: Well, you just did! See? It's contagious.

speaker: owl
text: No tests here! You *can't fail* in PhilWorld. You can only wonder.

speaker: owl
text: This world is made of *rooms*. Each holds one big idea. Talk to people and *touch things*, and the ideas will show themselves. You'll *hear* them too, so keep your ears open.

speaker: owl
text: Arrows or WASD to walk. *E* to interact. *M* opens the roadmap of ideas, *J* your journal, *H* asks me for a hint, *N* toggles sound.

speaker: owl
text: Before you choose a road, look at that *statue of a thinker* by the path. It's pondering the five biggest questions of all.

speaker: narrator
text: A stone figure sits chin-on-hand, frozen mid-thought. As you look closer, its questions seem to float up into the air…

speaker: owl
text: Those five questions are the main *branches* of philosophy. "Philosophy" itself comes from Greek: *philo* (love) + *sophia* (wisdom).

speaker: owl
text: Plato and Aristotle both said philosophy begins in *wonder*: being puzzled by things everyone else takes for granted.

speaker: owl
text: You earned your first *Insight*! Press *J* any time to reread it. Now the roads are open. *West* or *East*? Your choice!

speaker: alexander
text: I'm Alexander, prince of Macedon. Aristotle was hired by my father to tutor me, from when I was 13.

speaker: alexander
text: He taught me ethics, politics, poetry, medicine… and to always seek the *mean* between extremes.

speaker: alexander
text: Soon I'm going to conquer the known world, from Greece to India. He'd probably say I *slightly overshot* the mean on ambition.

speaker: aristotle
text: (calling over) An acorn! Plant it. Watch what it's *trying* to become.

speaker: aristotle
text: Every living thing has a *telos*: a built-in goal. The acorn's telos is to become a flourishing oak.

speaker: aristotle
text: And a human's? To use *reason* well and live a life of virtue together with others. I call that *eudaimonia*: flourishing, or deep happiness.

speaker: aristotle
text: Logic! I was the first to write down its rules. Here is a *syllogism*: two premises, one conclusion that MUST follow.

speaker: aristotle
text: Big circle: *mortal things*. Inside it: *humans*. Inside that: *Socrates*. If the circles are drawn right, the conclusion can't escape!

speaker: owl
text: His logic was the standard in Europe and the Islamic world for about 2,000 years. Thinkers like Ibn Sina and Ibn Rushd studied and expanded it.

speaker: aristotle
text: I dissected and described over *500 kinds of animals*. I noticed dolphins breathe air, give birth to live young and nurse them with milk.

speaker: aristotle
text: So they're more like land mammals than fish! Everyone laughed. About 2,000 years later, biologists agreed with me.

speaker: owl
text: Unlike Plato, Aristotle looked *down* at the world, not up. He collected, sorted and observed. He's often called the first great *scientist*.

speaker: aristotle
text: I sort everything: plants that *grow*, animals that grow and *feel and move*, and humans who grow, feel, move and *reason*.

speaker: aristotle
text: That tortoise and those sheep each have a *soul* in my sense: what makes a living thing alive and active. Not a ghost; more like its *way of being*.

speaker: aristotle
text: To truly understand *anything*, ask four "why" questions. I call them the *four causes*. Let's try them on this statue.

speaker: aristotle
text: 1. The *material* cause: what is it made of? *Marble.*

speaker: aristotle
text: 2. The *efficient* cause: what made it? *The sculptor's chisel*, tap, tap, tap.

speaker: aristotle
text: 3. The *formal* cause: what shape or design makes it *this* thing? *The form of a hero*, which the sculptor had in mind.

speaker: aristotle
text: 4. The *final* cause: what is it *for*? *To honor a hero*, and inspire citizens.

speaker: aristotle
text: Notice: for me the form isn't floating in some heaven like Plato's Forms. It's *in* the thing itself.

speaker: aristotle
text: Remember: virtue is a *habit*. You don't become kind by reading about kindness. You become kind by doing kind things, again and again.

speaker: aristotle
text: Ah, walk with me! My students are called *Peripatetics*: "the ones who walk around." I think better on my feet.

speaker: aristotle
text: My teacher Plato looked up to the heavens for truth. I look *here*: at animals, plants, cities, people. What actually makes a human life go *well*?

speaker: aristotle
text: My answer: *virtue*. And every virtue is a *mean* between two vices: one of too little, one of too much.

speaker: aristotle
text: Here. Tune these three virtues on this young soldier. Don't look for the exact middle. *Listen* for where it sounds right.

speaker: aristotle
text: You found them! Notice the mean wasn't always dead center. Courage leans a little toward boldness, generosity a little toward caution. The mean is *relative to us* and to the situation.

speaker: aristotle
text: That takes *practical wisdom*, phronesis. No rulebook can do it for you.

speaker: aristotle
text: And virtue is a *habit*. A harpist becomes good by playing the harp; we become brave by doing brave things. Do it until it's who you are.

speaker: owl
text: The path *west* to the Stoa is open, and so is the other road back at the Agora.

speaker: narrator
text: A small rented room in Sils-Maria. A desk, piles of notebooks, medicine bottles, and a pair of very worn walking boots.

speaker: nietzsche
text: I walk six, eight hours a day here. *"All truly great thoughts are conceived while walking."*

speaker: owl
text: Nietzsche suffered terrible headaches, stomach pain and near-blindness for most of his life. He wrote anyway, often in short bursts. Pain was something he tried to say *yes* to.

speaker: narrator
text: A huge pyramid-shaped boulder by Lake Silvaplana. Nietzsche said a thought struck him right here in August 1881, "6,000 feet beyond man and time."

speaker: narrator
text: Darkness, all the way down. Then two red eyes blink open, looking back up at you.

speaker: nietzsche
text: *"Whoever fights monsters should see to it that he does not become a monster. And if you gaze long into an abyss, the abyss also gazes into you."*

speaker: narrator
text: Already cracked.

speaker: nietzsche
text: In my book *Thus Spoke Zarathustra*, the spirit goes through *three transformations*.

speaker: nietzsche
text: First, the *camel*. It kneels and says: "Load me up!" It carries all the heavy values it was handed: duty, tradition, *"Thou shalt."*

speaker: nietzsche
text: Then the *lion*. In the desert it meets a great dragon whose every scale reads *"Thou shalt."* The lion roars: *"I will!"* It wins its freedom by saying *No*.

speaker: nietzsche
text: But the lion can't *create*. So last comes the *child*: innocence, forgetting, a game, a new beginning, a sacred *Yes*. The child makes *new* values.

speaker: nietzsche
text: Hear a story I wrote, in *The Gay Science* (1882). Watch.

speaker: narrator
text: On a bright morning, a madman lights a lantern and runs into the marketplace…

speaker: name:The Madman
text: "I seek God! I seek God!"

speaker: narrator
text: The people there don't believe in God anymore. They laugh. "Did he get lost? Did he emigrate? Is he hiding?"

speaker: name:The Madman
text: "Where is God? I will tell you. *We have killed him*, you and I. *God is dead.* God remains dead."

speaker: name:The Madman
text: "I have come too early. This tremendous event is still on its way…"

speaker: nietzsche
text: Don't mistake me. I'm not *cheering*. I'm describing something: in modern Europe, people no longer truly *live by* the old beliefs, yet they still lean on the values those beliefs held up.

speaker: nietzsche
text: The madman says he came *too early*. Nobody yet sees what it means: if the foundation is gone, what holds up *meaning*, *morality*, *truth*?

speaker: owl
text: People still argue about this today. Many religious thinkers strongly disagree with Nietzsche, and that argument is part of philosophy too.

speaker: nietzsche
text: Ah, a visitor on my mountain! I am Friedrich Nietzsche. Excuse the mustache. It has its own opinions.

speaker: nietzsche
text: So. Take this hammer. I *philosophize with a hammer*. Not to smash things blindly, but to *tap* the great idols, like a tuning fork, and hear whether they ring *hollow*.

speaker: nietzsche
text: Those three gleaming pillars on the ledge: tap each one. Listen closely.

speaker: nietzsche
text: Tap them! All three. Don't be afraid of what you hear.

speaker: nietzsche
text: One more test, the heaviest. Go sit by the *pyramid rock* by the lake. That's where this thought first came to me.

speaker: nietzsche
text: Well, friend?

speaker: nietzsche
text: The *Übermensch*, the "Overhuman," is an ideal: someone who creates their own values and says *yes* to life, with all its suffering.

speaker: nietzsche
text: "Man is a rope stretched between animal and Übermensch: a rope over an abyss." Ha! You'll see that rope soon.

speaker: nietzsche
text: Terribly. After my mind collapsed in 1889, my sister edited my notes and later bent my ideas to fit German nationalism and antisemitism, which *I despised*.

speaker: owl
text: True. Nietzsche wrote openly against antisemites, and fell out with his old friend Wagner partly over it. Scholars spent decades rescuing his real ideas.

speaker: narrator
text: CRASH. The pillars topple and shatter in the snow. Cold wind howls through the empty space where they stood.

speaker: nietzsche
text: There. Do you feel it? Dizziness. As if we're falling in every direction. If nothing is *given* from above, does anything matter at all?

speaker: nietzsche
text: That feeling is *nihilism*: "nothing has value." It's the great danger of our age. But it is *not* the end of the story.

speaker: nietzsche
text: If values aren't handed down to us, then we must *create* them. That is the task: *become who you are*.

speaker: nietzsche
text: Now, one last test, the heaviest of all. Go sit by the *pyramid rock* by the lake.

speaker: demon
text: …What if, one day or night, a *demon* crept after you into your loneliest loneliness and said:

speaker: demon
text: "This life, as you now live it, you will have to live *once more*, and *innumerable times more*. Every pain, every joy, every thought and sigh, all in the same order."

speaker: demon
text: "Even this spider, and this moonlight between the trees. Even this moment, and I myself. The eternal hourglass of existence, turned over again and again, and you with it, speck of dust!"

speaker: narrator
text: How do you answer the demon?

speaker: demon
text: Again. The same pains. The same regrets. The same small, grey days. Forever.

speaker: nietzsche
text: Feel how heavy that is? Then the real question is not "is it true?" It's this: *how would you have to live, so that you could say yes to it?*

speaker: narrator
text: Then…

speaker: nietzsche
text: YES! Hear it? The very same melody, but now you *love* it. Nothing changed except your *yes*.

speaker: nietzsche
text: That is *amor fati*: love of fate. Not just putting up with what happens, but *loving* it, even the hard parts. Wanting nothing to be different, not forward, not backward, not in all eternity.

speaker: nietzsche
text: Look: a *rope* now stretches across the abyss. "Man is a rope over an abyss." Cross it. On the other side, some Parisians have been reading me very closely…

speaker: narrator
text: An hourglass, its sand slowly running out. Beside it, an open notebook in Greek.

speaker: narrator
text: On the hourglass is carved: *MEMENTO MORI*, "remember that you will die."

speaker: marcus
text: Not to be gloomy. To be *awake*. If today were your last, would you spend it complaining about traffic?

speaker: owl
text: The Stoics also practiced *premeditatio malorum*: calmly imagining losses in advance, so they wouldn't be crushed by surprise and would appreciate what they have.

speaker: narrator
text: A letter signed *Seneca*: Roman statesman, playwright, and Stoic. He wrote 124 letters of advice to his friend Lucilius.

speaker: narrator
text: "We suffer more often in *imagination* than in reality." Most of our fears are about things that never actually happen.

speaker: owl
text: The Roman orator Cicero described a *Stoic archer*. Do everything you can to aim well. Then let go.

speaker: narrator
text: A sudden gust pushes the arrow wide. A miss!

speaker: narrator
text: THUNK! Bullseye!

speaker: owl
text: Either way, the Stoic asks only: *did I aim well?* The aim was up to you; the wind wasn't. Hitting is "preferred," but your aim is your *success*.

speaker: epictetus
text: Yes, friend?

speaker: epictetus
text: Some things are up to us: our judgments, choices and efforts. The rest is not. Don't tie your peace to the second list.

speaker: epictetus
text: Sit, sit. My teaching fits in one sentence, the very first line of my *Handbook*:

speaker: epictetus
text: *"Some things are up to us, and some things are not up to us."*

speaker: epictetus
text: Most misery comes from mixing them up. Let's practice. I'll toss things to you. Sort each one: *← not up to me* or *→ up to me*.

speaker: epictetus
text: Good. Now listen: *"People are disturbed not by things, but by their judgments about things."*

speaker: epictetus
text: An insult is just sounds. The *story* you tell about it is what hurts, and that story is up to you.

speaker: epictetus
text: Go see the Emperor Marcus by his tent. I think… the weather is about to give you a test.

speaker: marcus
text: Greetings. I am Marcus Aurelius, Emperor of Rome. Forgive me, I'm writing in my notebook. Talk to Epictetus first. His books taught me most of what I know.

speaker: marcus
text: Yes?

speaker: marcus
text: Notes to myself. Never meant for anyone else. People will later publish them as my *Meditations*.

speaker: marcus
text: Ah, you've learned the sorting. Now let's see it in the body, not just the head. Look at the sea.

speaker: marcus
text: A storm. You cannot stop it. You cannot argue with it. Not even an emperor can.

speaker: marcus
text: But *inside* you there is a citadel the storm cannot enter, unless you open the gates. Breathe with me.

speaker: marcus
text: Listen. The storm is still roaring… but it isn't *inside* you anymore.

speaker: marcus
text: I wrote in my notebook: *"You have power over your mind, not outside events. Realize this, and you will find strength."*

speaker: marcus
text: And there, the sun. It too was never up to you. Enjoy it anyway!

speaker: owl
text: The path *up* at the end of the colonnade is open. Where it leads, about 1,700 years later, a philosopher will challenge *everything*, including the Stoics.

speaker: zeno
text: I'm Zeno, founder of this school. We meet here at the *Stoa Poikile*, the "Painted Porch." That's why they call us *Stoics*.

speaker: zeno
text: Want to know how I became a philosopher? It began with a disaster.

speaker: narrator
text: A wealthy merchant sails toward Athens, his ship heavy with precious purple dye.

speaker: zeno
text: A storm! The waves are too high!

speaker: narrator
text: The ship sinks with everything he owns.

speaker: narrator
text: Penniless in Athens, he wanders into a bookshop and picks up a book about *Socrates*.

speaker: zeno
text: "Where can I find a man like this?" I asked. The bookseller pointed to a philosopher walking by. *Follow him*, he said. And I did.

speaker: zeno
text: Later I said: *"I made a prosperous voyage when I suffered shipwreck."* Losing everything showed me what truly mattered.

speaker: epictetus
text: I was born a *slave*. My name even means "acquired." Let me show you a story they tell about me.

speaker: name:His Master
text: Let's see if you cry out, philosopher.

speaker: epictetus
text: (calmly) If you keep twisting, you'll break it.

speaker: epictetus
text: (just as calmly) There. Didn't I tell you?

speaker: epictetus
text: Perhaps it's only a legend. But the lesson is true: my leg was never up to me. My *response* was. Later I was freed and taught philosophy in Rome and Greece.

speaker: marcus
text: Each morning I write: today I will meet people who are rude, ungrateful, dishonest. Let me show you one such morning.

speaker: marcus
text: They act that way out of ignorance. I can't be harmed by them unless I *choose* to be. And I was born to work *with* them, like hands and feet.

speaker: owl
text: The most powerful man in the world, fighting wars and plague, writing himself reminders to be patient.

speaker: narrator
text: A hard grey stone with a deep, smooth groove worn into its top, right beneath a dripping spring.

speaker: laozi
text: *"Nothing in the world is softer or weaker than water. Yet for attacking the hard and strong, nothing can beat it."*

speaker: laozi
text: Drip by drip, century by century, the soft overcomes the hard. Not by force, but by *persistence* and *yielding*.

speaker: narrator
text: You turn the stone. The sky begins to shift…

speaker: laozi
text: *Yin* and *yang*. Dark and light, soft and hard, rest and motion. Not enemies: partners. Each contains the seed of the other, and each turns into the other.

speaker: laozi
text: Hear the low tone and the high tone? Alone, each is thin. Together: harmony. *"When everyone knows beauty as beauty, ugliness is already there."* No high without low.

speaker: narrator
text: You pour water into a clay pot. It fills up the empty space inside.

speaker: laozi
text: *"Thirty spokes share one hub; it is the empty center that makes the wheel useful. Shape clay into a pot; it is the emptiness inside that makes it useful."*

speaker: laozi
text: Everyone admires what *is*. Few notice the power of what *isn't*: the empty room you live in, the silence between notes, the pause before a reply.

speaker: narrator
text: A rough, uncarved block of wood.

speaker: laozi
text: *Pu*, the uncarved block. Before it's carved into a bowl or a spoon, it could become *anything*. Simplicity is full of possibility.

speaker: laozi
text: Be like the block: unpretentious, natural, not carved up by ambition and cleverness.

speaker: narrator
text: The opening line of the *Tao Te Ching*, said to be written by Laozi on his way out of China.

speaker: narrator
text: As you read it… the words fade away.

speaker: laozi
text: The *Tao*, "the Way," is the source and flow of everything. The moment you put it into words, you've made it smaller. Like trying to hold water in your fist.

speaker: laozi
text: Mm. A traveler. I am called *Laozi*, "the Old Master." Legend says I was keeper of the royal archives, until I grew tired of court life and rode west on this buffalo.

speaker: owl
text: Historians aren't sure Laozi was even one real person! The Tao Te Ching may be a collection by several hands. The legend is still lovely.

speaker: laozi
text: You want to reach the *next valley*? The river goes there. Take the little boat at the dock. Paddle hard!

speaker: laozi
text: The boat is waiting at the dock.

speaker: laozi
text: Mm?

speaker: laozi
text: *"Governing a large country is like cooking a small fish."* Poke at it too much and it falls apart. The best leaders are barely noticed. When their work is done, the people say: "We did it ourselves."

speaker: laozi
text: Ha! The farmer who pulls on his rice shoots to help them grow faster kills them. The lazy farmer lets weeds win. Wu wei is the *third way*: tend, then trust. Act, but don't force.

speaker: narrator
text: The river sparkles. You've already learned what it had to teach.

speaker: laozi
text: Reach the far valley. Use the *arrow keys* to paddle. Paddle hard!

speaker: narrator
text: The boat glides gently onto a sandy bank. You arrived without even trying, once you stopped trying.

speaker: laozi
text: Ha! You didn't even pick up the paddle. You're a natural. Most people fight for years before learning that.

speaker: laozi
text: Notice what happened. The harder you paddled, the more you got stuck, spun around and crashed. When you let go, the current carried you *around* every rock.

speaker: laozi
text: This is *wu wei*: "non-action," or better, *effortless action*. Not doing nothing. Acting *with* the flow of things, like a swimmer using the current instead of fighting it.

speaker: laozi
text: *"The Tao does nothing, yet nothing is left undone."* The seasons turn, the rivers run, the plants grow. No strain, no fuss.

speaker: owl
text: The path *east* toward the Bodhi Tree is open. Laozi's ideas will later blend with Buddhism in China, giving rise to *Chan*, known in Japan as *Zen*!

speaker: zhuangzi
text: Mmm… zzz… ah! Oh. I'm *Zhuangzi*. Sorry, I was dreaming. Want to try? Close your eyes…

speaker: zhuangzi
text: Once I, Zhuangzi, dreamt I was a butterfly, fluttering happily, with no idea I was Zhuangzi.

speaker: zhuangzi
text: Suddenly I woke up, and there I was, solidly Zhuangzi. But now I can't tell: *was I Zhuangzi dreaming I was a butterfly, or am I a butterfly dreaming I'm Zhuangzi?*

speaker: zhuangzi
text: Maybe the boundaries we draw, between me and not-me, dream and waking, are less fixed than we think. Things keep *transforming* into each other.

speaker: name:The Gatekeeper
text: Old Master! You're leaving the kingdom forever? Then please, before you go, *write down your wisdom* for us!

speaker: narrator
text: Laozi writes about 5,000 characters in two short books. The *Tao Te Ching*: "The Classic of the Way and Its Power."

speaker: narrator
text: Then he rides west through the gate… and is never seen again.

speaker: cookding

speaker: confucius
text: How should a *ruler* and a *minister* treat each other?

speaker: confucius
text: Blind obedience isn't loyalty! A good minister *speaks up* when the ruler is wrong, respectfully but honestly.

speaker: confucius
text: The ruler leads by virtue; the minister serves loyally and speaks up.

speaker: confucius
text: "Govern by virtue and you will be like the North Star: it stays in place while all the other stars turn around it."

speaker: confucius
text: Then the state falls apart. Rulers who serve only themselves lose the people's trust, and without trust no state can stand.

speaker: confucius
text: How should a *parent* and a *child* treat each other?

speaker: confucius
text: Fear isn't respect. Confucius said even dogs and horses get fed. What matters is *reverence* and care, given willingly.

speaker: confucius
text: For Confucius, the family is where we *first* learn to be human. It's the root of every other virtue.

speaker: confucius
text: The parent cares and guides; the child respects, and cares for them when they're old.

speaker: confucius
text: This is *xiao*, filial piety: love and respect flowing up, care and guidance flowing down.

speaker: confucius
text: How should an *elder* and a *younger* sibling treat each other?

speaker: confucius
text: Kindness from above, respect from below. Each role carries a *duty*, not just a privilege.

speaker: confucius
text: Bossing isn't leading. An elder who isn't kind hasn't earned the younger's respect.

speaker: confucius
text: A family at war with itself can't teach harmony to anyone else.

speaker: confucius
text: How should *spouses* treat each other?

speaker: confucius
text: In Confucius's day these roles were *unequal*, and later thinkers argued hard about that. The core idea that survives: duties flow *both ways*.

speaker: confucius
text: How should *friends* treat each other?

speaker: confucius
text: Confucius warned against friends who flatter. A true friend tells you the truth, kindly.

speaker: confucius
text: Friends are equals who are trustworthy and help each other grow.

speaker: confucius
text: The only relationship of *equals* among the five. "Have no friends who are not as good as yourself": friends lift each other up.

speaker: socrates
text: Interesting! This is what old Cephalus says in Plato's *Republic*. Let's test it.

speaker: socrates
text: Suppose a friend lends you his sword. Later he goes *mad* and demands it back, raging.

speaker: socrates
text: You owe it to him. Is it *just* to hand a sword to a madman?

speaker: socrates
text: Interesting! Polemarchus argues this in the *Republic*. Let's test it.

speaker: socrates
text: But we often misjudge who our friends really are. Someone who seems friendly might be robbing you!

speaker: socrates
text: And tell me: does *harming* a person make them better, or worse? Can justice ever make people *worse*?

speaker: socrates
text: Interesting! Thrasymachus angrily says this in the *Republic*. Let's test it.

speaker: socrates
text: But rulers make *mistakes*. Sometimes they order things that actually harm themselves.

speaker: socrates
text: Then obeying them is sometimes *not* in the stronger's interest. So is justice obeying, or benefiting? It can't be both!

speaker: buddha
text: Life involves *dukkha*: suffering, dissatisfaction, a sense that something is never quite right.

speaker: buddha
text: Its cause is *tanha*: craving and clinging, to pleasure, to being, even to not-being.

speaker: buddha
text: Suffering *can end*. That ending is *nirvana*: literally "blowing out," like a flame of craving gone quiet.

speaker: buddha
text: The *Eightfold Path*: right view, intention, speech, action, livelihood, effort, mindfulness, concentration.

speaker: narrator
text:
*Metaphysics* asks: What is *REAL*?
Is the world just atoms? Do minds exist? What is time?

speaker: narrator
text:
*Epistemology* asks: How do I *KNOW*?
Can I trust my senses? What counts as proof? Could I be dreaming?

speaker: narrator
text:
*Ethics* asks: What *SHOULD* I do?
What makes an action right? What is a good life? What do we owe each other?

speaker: narrator
text:
*Logic* asks: What makes reasoning *GOOD*?
When does one idea really follow from another? How do we spot bad arguments?

speaker: narrator
text:
*Aesthetics* asks: What is *BEAUTY*?
Is beauty in the object or in the eye? Why does music move us?

speaker: name:Channa, the charioteer
text: He is *sick*, my prince. Anyone can fall ill, even a king.

speaker: name:Prince Siddhartha
text: Why are they carrying that still body, weeping?

speaker: name:Channa, the charioteer

speaker: name:Prince Siddhartha

speaker: name:Channa, the charioteer
